sections.learningObjectives:
- Explain the purpose of the electrocardiogram (ECG) and what it records.
- Describe limb-lead and chest (precordial) lead-placement concepts and landmarks.
- Prepare the patient and equipment for an ECG while protecting privacy and reducing artifact.
- Apply scope boundaries by supporting the ECG procedure, escalating urgent symptoms, and never interpreting the tracing.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

The ECG is like taking a picture of the heart's electric rhythm so the doctor can look at it. It gathers information; it does not fix anything by itself.

### Question 2

EKG and ECG are two names for the very same test, like saying “bike” or “bicycle.”

### Question 3

Having an ECG is like wearing little stickers on your skin. The stickers listen to your heart, but they do not poke, pinch, or zap you.

### Question 4

There are 10 sticky pads but 12 “views” of the heart. Some pads team up with others to make extra views, like two people making several different shadow shapes on a wall.

### Question 5

Twelve is how many different “angles” the machine uses to look at the heart's electricity, not how many stickers or minutes there are.

### Question 6

An electrode is like a tiny microphone sticker. It sits on the skin and hears the heart's electric signals so the machine can draw them.

### Question 7

Imagine trying to understand a big 3D shape. Looking at it from the front, side, and top gives you the whole picture. The leads do the same for the heart.

### Question 8

When someone's chest hurts, their heart beats strangely, or they feel out of breath, the ECG helps the doctor peek at the heart's electric rhythm.

### Question 9

An ECG is one of the easiest tests: you just lie still for a few seconds while stickers listen to your heart. No needles, no pain, no rays.

### Question 10

The four limb stickers go on the two arms and two legs, one each — like putting a badge on each of your four corners.

### Question 11

The limb stickers go near the ends of the arms and legs, like wearing four stretchy bracelets and anklets that listen to your heart.

### Question 12

There is a color code to help you put each limb sticker in the right spot: right arm = white, like the first color of the flag you remember.

### Question 13

Left leg = red, like a red sock on the left foot. The colors are a cheat code to get every sticker in the right place.

### Question 14

The right-leg sticker is like the “steady hand” that keeps the picture from wobbling, so the other stickers can draw a clean line.

### Question 15

Left arm = black, like a black wristband on the left wrist. The color code helps you avoid mixing up the two arms.

### Question 16

Think of the limb stickers as looking at the heart from the front of the body, straight on — like a camera held in front of your chest.

### Question 17

If you put the left and right arm stickers on the wrong arms, the machine draws a backwards picture. It is not the patient's heart that is wrong — just the stickers.

### Question 18

Stickers stick best to clean, dry, smooth skin — like tape sticks better to a dry table than a greasy one.

### Question 19

V1 sits just to the right of the breastbone, at the level of the fourth little gap between the ribs.

### Question 20

V1 and V2 are like a pair: one sits on each side of the breastbone at the same level, like two bookends.

### Question 21

V4 sits in the fifth rib gap, straight down from the middle of the collarbone on the left side.

### Question 22

V3 goes exactly halfway between V2 and V4 — like placing a dot in the middle of a line you already drew.

### Question 23

V5 sits on the side of the chest, in line with the front fold of the armpit, at the same height as V4.

### Question 24

V6 sits on the side of the chest under the middle of the armpit, at the same height as V4.

### Question 25

“Precordial” is just a fancy word for “near the heart on the chest.” The six V stickers are the precordial leads.

### Question 26

To find the right spot, find the little bump where the breastbone angles — that is your starting line — then count the rib gaps down from there.

### Question 27

Place the two bookends by the breastbone, then the one under the collarbone line, then fill in the middle, then the two on the side — like a connect-the-dots picture.

### Question 28

The six V stickers go on the front and left side of the chest, like a curved row of buttons over the ribs.

### Question 29

V4, V5, and V6 all sit on the same horizontal shelf, like three buttons sewn in a straight row across the chest.

### Question 30

Picture a string hanging straight down from the middle of your collarbone — that is the midclavicular line.

### Question 31

Moving a V sticker even a little is like moving a camera a few steps — the photo looks different even though the scene is the same.

### Question 32

When the map is hard to read, you ask the person who knows the area for directions instead of guessing.

### Question 33

Put your finger in the front crease of your armpit and draw a straight line up and down — that is the anterior axillary line.

### Question 34

Before doing anything, make sure you have the right person and tell them what is about to happen — like checking the name on a package before opening it.

### Question 35

To put the stickers on the chest, the patient changes into a hospital gown — like changing into a swimsuit cover-up before going in the water.

### Question 36

Stickers need a clean, dry spot to work, just like a bandage sticks best to dry skin.

### Question 37

Greasy skin is like a slippery floor for stickers — wipe it clean so they can grip and do their job.

### Question 38

Hairy skin is like a shaggy carpet — you may need to trim it a little so the sticker can reach the floor, but only with the patient's okay and the office's rules.

### Question 39

The patient lies back like they are about to rest, because still and relaxed muscles make the cleanest picture.

### Question 40

To get a clear picture, the patient plays a game of “freeze” for a few seconds — still body, quiet voice, easy breathing.

### Question 41

Wiggling while the machine draws is like shaking the paper while someone draws a straight line — the line comes out wobbly.

### Question 42

When you talk, your chest muscles wiggle too — like a shaky hand trying to draw — so we ask for a few quiet seconds.

### Question 43

Shivering is like the whole body shaking the drawing board — keeping the patient cozy keeps the picture steady.

### Question 44

Metal objects can act like little antennas that add static to the picture, so we set them aside during the test.

### Question 45

We cover up everything we do not need to see, just like a changing screen at a swimming pool, so the patient feels safe and respected.

### Question 46

The honest answer is like explaining a sticker on your hand: it just sits there and does not hurt at all.

### Question 47

The assistant writes down the important notes, like listing the ingredients, but the chef (the clinician) decides what the recipe means.

### Question 48

A test needs a doctor's “go” before it happens — like needing a coach's signal before starting a play.

### Question 49

Before the test, check your tools the way you would check a flashlight's batteries before a campout.

### Question 50

The assistant is like the camera operator who sets up the shot and hands the photo to the doctor, who is the one who reads it.

### Question 51

After taking the picture, make sure it is clear and has the right name on it, then hand it to the doctor to read.

### Question 52

If a patient says their chest hurts, that is a “fire alarm” moment — stop and call for help right away.

### Question 53

The assistant is not the one who reads the picture — they hand anything that looks odd to the person who is trained to read it.

### Question 54

Only the doctor (or another licensed clinician) is the one who reads the heart's picture and explains what it means.

### Question 55

When someone asks what a picture means, the assistant says the doctor will read it and explain — the assistant does not guess.

### Question 56

The assistant writes down the who, when, and what happened — like filling in a scorecard — but the doctor writes the final “what it means.”

### Question 57

If the stickers will not stick, check the skin and the stickers, and if it still will not work, ask a teammate for help.

### Question 58

When you are not sure where a piece goes, ask someone who knows instead of guessing — like asking for directions instead of taking a wrong turn.

### Question 59

A good sticker is fresh and sticky, like a new bandage from a sealed packet, not an old dried-out one.

### Question 60

Check that the sticker's gooey center is still moist and sticky — a dried sticker will not listen well.

### Question 61

Lead wires are the cords that carry the heart's electric signals from the stickers to the machine, like wires carrying sound from a microphone to a speaker.

### Question 62

The ground electrode is like the steady anchor that keeps the whole picture from shaking with static.

### Question 63

The ECG listens to electricity, not to how hard the heart squeezes or how hard blood pushes. Those need different tools.

### Question 64

ECG = electricity. Blood pressure = how hard the blood pushes. Two different measuring sticks for two different things.

### Question 65

A clear picture needs two things: stickers that stick well, and a person who stays still.

### Question 66

Four limb stickers can team up to make six different views, and the six chest stickers make six more — ten stickers, twelve views.

### Question 67

The standard limb leads are named with plain numbers: I, II, and III.

### Question 68

The augmented leads are the ones with the little “a” in front: aVR, aVL, and aVF.

### Question 69

Lead II is like the camera angle that usually gives the clearest view of the heartbeat, so monitors often use it.

### Question 70

The chest stickers look at the heart going around the body sideways, like walking around a statue to see every side.

### Question 71

The limb stickers look at the heart from straight on, like a camera held in front of the chest.

### Question 72

Wet skin makes stickers slide right off — dry it first, like drying a dish before putting a sticker on it.

### Question 73

Stickers work best on smooth, soft ground — not on bumpy rocks (bones) or wobbly ground (muscles).

### Question 74

If a patient feels dizzy, help them stay safe and call for the doctor right away — like catching someone who is about to tip over.

### Question 75

The ECG is like a detective's clue that can show if the heart's rhythm is off or if part of the heart is hungry for blood.

### Question 76

A test only happens when the doctor says to do it, not because anyone in the office feels like it.

### Question 77

Label the picture with the patient's name and the time it was taken, like writing your name on your homework before turning it in.

### Question 78

After labeling the picture, put it in the patient's folder so the doctor can find it and read it later.

### Question 79

The ECG checks the heart's beat and its electric wiring, like a mechanic checking a car's engine timing.

### Question 80

When you know what is going to happen, you feel calmer — and a calm, still person makes the clearest picture.

### Question 81

If the line gets wobbly right after a cough, it is the body moving the pen, not the heart changing — fix the wiggles and try again.

### Question 82

The assistant sets up and runs the camera and labels the photo; the doctor reads the photo and explains it.

### Question 83

Reading the heart's picture and explaining it is the doctor's job, not the assistant's — like only the teacher grades the test.

### Question 84

ECG = the heart's electric wiring. Echo = sound waves that make a movie of the heart. Same heart, different cameras.
